source.filename: 2025-Toward a deeper understanding of layer jamming structures.pdf

constitutive_assumptions: Planar stress state assumed for all material points within the LJS beam
Layers are assumed to be composed of linear elastic material
Axial force (N) influence on extensional stress distribution and bending deformation is omitted
Interlayer sliding surfaces obey Coulomb friction where shear stress equals sign(Q)*μ*p
Friction coefficient (μ) is treated as constant
Sliding region boundary ys is treated as a continuous variable rather than discrete steps to ensure smooth expansion and continuous stress changes
Radius of curvature is assumed sufficiently large and distributed axial load qs is non-zero only at discrete points, making (1/(b*h))*dN/ds negligible in layer stress equilibrium
Second-order small quantities are neglected and small angle approximations cos(dθ) ≈ 1 and sin(dθ) ≈ dθ are applied for differential beam segment equilibrium
control_variables: Beam total height (5 mm for FEA / 5.1 mm for experimental beams)
Beam length / arc length (100 mm for straight beams, 150 mm arc length for curved beams)
Thermoplastic forming conditions for curved specimens (heated at 70 °C for 1 h)
Deflection limit during monotonic cantilever testing (5 mm)
Number of repetitions per monotonic test condition (5 repetitions to compute mean and standard deviation)
Deflection range for cyclic loading tests (alternating between 3 mm and -3 mm over 5 cycles)
dependent_variables: Extensional stress distribution (σ) and shear stress distribution (τ)
Sliding boundary position (ys) across the beam cross section
Critical shear force / critical load for sliding onset (Qcr)
Beam deflection and angular deformation (w, Δθ)
Frictional energy dissipation / load-deflection hysteresis loop area

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: In layer jamming beams under bending, interlayer sliding initiates at the central layers when shear stress reaches the frictional limit, producing three distinct cross-sectional regimes: full jamming, half jamming, and full sliding.
evidence_relevant_to_topic.evidence_type: Numerical finite element analysis and analytical derivation

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: The critical load and critical shear force required to initiate layer sliding scale proportionally with the applied hydrostatic vacuum pressure.
Varying layer thickness does not substantially affect initial pre-sliding bending stiffness, but post-sliding bending stiffness is significantly higher in beams constructed with thicker layers.
evidence_relevant_to_topic.evidence_type: Experimental cantilever testing and theoretical modeling

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Curved layer jamming beams display a progressive, smooth decrease in bending stiffness during deformation without the sharp stiffness transitions typical of straight beams, because initial curvature alters the equivalent moment of inertia.
evidence_relevant_to_topic.evidence_type: Analytical model formulation and experimental validation

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Cyclic loading of layer jamming beams creates closed load-deflection hysteresis loops representing energy dissipation through interlayer friction, which can be captured by tracking stress increments in an iterative algorithm.
evidence_relevant_to_topic.evidence_type: Iterative algorithm simulation and experimental cyclic testing

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: The equivalent moment of inertia of a straight layer jamming beam bounds between a solid-like upper limit (b*h^3/12) in the full-jamming state and a liquid-like lower limit (b*delta^2*h/12) in the full-sliding state.

experimental_setup: Freely sliding holding frame on a rail to eliminate horizontal constraints during bending
Tensile testing machine fitted with a force sensor to record load and deflection
Vacuum regulation system comprising a vacuum pump and a vacuum proportional valve

Straight LJS cantilevers and simply supported beams made of stacked PVC sheets inside a polyethylene vacuum bag (lengths: 100 mm; width: 20 mm; height: 5 mm/5.1 mm; layer thicknesses: 0.3 mm, 0.5 mm, 1.0 mm)

Curved LJS specimens formed by thermoplastic forming of PVC sheets at 70 °C for 1 h (semicircular arc with 47.75 mm radius, quarter-circular arc with 95.50 mm radius, arc length: 150 mm, width: 20 mm, height: 5.1 mm, layer thickness: 0.3 mm)
Cantilever fixture testing at 40, 70, and 100 kPa hydrostatic pressures
Simply supported cyclic loading fixture alternating deflections between 3 mm and -3 mm at 100 kPa hydrostatic pressure
future_work: Extending the analytical modeling methodology from beam-stack LJS to shell-stack LJS and other jamming configurations involving bending deformations
Applying the model to structural design and optimization of soft robotic systems, prosthetics, and controllable-stiffness mechanisms
independent_variables: Hydrostatic vacuum pressure (40 kPa, 70 kPa, 100 kPa)
Beam geometry / initial curvature (straight beam, semicircular curved beam, quarter-circular curved beam)
Support and boundary conditions (cantilever, simply supported)
Loading mode (monotonic deflection to 5 mm, cyclic loading between 3 mm and -3 mm)
limitations_inferred: Quasi-static testing does not account for dynamic loading rates, rate-dependent friction, or viscoelastic relaxation of the PVC sheets and polyethylene envelope.
Constitutive parameters (friction coefficient μ and Young's modulus E) were fitted from a single specimen response rather than measured independently via standard tribological and tensile tests.
The modeling framework is restricted to planar 2D bending and does not consider out-of-plane, torsional, or coupled multi-axial deformations.
Durability was only evaluated over 5 cycles, leaving long-term wear of layer interfaces and vacuum envelope integrity unaddressed.
limitations_stated_by_authors: The theoretical model tends to overestimate critical load values, particularly at low hydrostatic pressures and when layers are thin.
Imperfections during specimen fabrication prevent vacuum pressure from distributing completely uniformly across layer contact surfaces.
Theoretical frictional energy dissipation during cyclic loading is smaller than experimental measurements.
Discrepancies and distortions occur near zero load during cyclic loading due to low support stiffness of the simply supported ends in the experimental setup.
The mathematical derivation is specifically developed for beam-stack LJS under planar bending.
Treating the sliding layer boundary (ys) as a continuous variable rather than discrete layer interfaces is an approximation that averages internal force changes across sliding layers.
Axial force and interlayer normal strain are neglected in the deformation equations.
main_results: Identified three distinct mechanical states in layer jamming beams (full jamming, half jamming, and full sliding) and established closed-form stress and stress increment distributions.
Derived a closed-form quadratic approximation connecting the interlayer sliding boundary (ys) to shear force (Q), resolving the implicit transcendental relationship.
Formulated a governing differential equation for angular deformation and an iterative algorithm based on stress increments that solves large deformations and cyclic loading.
Demonstrated that critical sliding loads are directly proportional to applied hydrostatic pressure in both model predictions and experimental measurements.
Showed that layer thickness has negligible influence on initial elastic stiffness but significantly enhances post-sliding bending stiffness.

Demonstrated that curved LJS beams experience smooth, continuous stiffness reductions rather than sharp transitions upon layer sliding due to the influence of curvature on equivalent moment of inertia.
Confirmed energy dissipation through interlayer friction during cyclic loading via experimental hysteresis loops, which were qualitatively reproduced by the iterative algorithm.
modeling_methods: Finite element analysis (FEA) in Abaqus using 2D CPS4R elements under plane stress conditions
Euler-Bernoulli beam theory extended to multi-layer composite beams with interlayer friction and sliding
Cross-sectional stress distribution formulation for full-jamming, half-jamming, and full-sliding regimes
Internal force equilibrium differential equations for curved continuous medium beams
Quadratic closed-form approximation for the sliding boundary ys as a function of shear force Q
Governing differential equation for angular deformation increment (Δθ') derived from strain compatibility and constitutive relations
Iterative multi-step algorithm based on stress increments for large deformations and non-monotonic loading
Equivalent moment of inertia (Ieq) formulation across sliding states
performance_metrics: Critical load and critical shear force (Qcr) for sliding initiation
Equivalent moment of inertia (Ieq, Ieq_max, Ieq_min)
Load-deflection hysteresis loop area (frictional energy dissipation)
Theoretical-to-experimental correlation across varying pressures and layer thicknesses
possible_gap_implications: The closed-form governing equation and iterative algorithm provide an analytical tool that could replace empirical tuning in the design and shape control of variable-stiffness soft robotic limbs, grippers, and continuum manipulators.
The validated frictional hysteresis model could guide the development of tunable dampers, vibration isolators, and energy-absorbing wearable robotics/prosthetics.

The observed discrepancies resulting from contact pressure non-uniformity and fixture compliance highlight a research gap in soft-interface packaging, uniform vacuum distribution, and compliant boundary condition modeling.
paper.research_objective: To develop a closed-form deformation model and governing equation for beam-stack layer jamming structures (LJS) applicable to both straight and curved beams under complex loading, analyze internal stress distributions and increments via finite element analysis, and experimentally validate the model's accuracy under varying layer thicknesses, hydrostatic pressures, and cyclic loading.
paper.research_problem: Complex interlayer friction and sliding interactions in layer jamming structures (LJS) make their mechanical behavior highly nonlinear, impeding the development of comprehensive closed-form models and leaving LJS design largely dependent on empirical experience, while existing models are mostly restricted to straight beams under specific conditions and suffer from heavy computational demands.
paper.robot_type: Layer jamming structure (LJS) beam (the paper investigates variable-stiffness layer jamming structure beam elements for soft robotics rather than a complete robotic device)
paper.title: Toward a deeper understanding of layer jamming structures
